title: Who Decides What a Urinal Is Worth?
paragraphs: In nineteen seventeen, Marcel Duchamp submitted a porcelain urinal, signed R. Mutt and titled Fountain, to a New York exhibition that promised to show any work whose artist paid the fee. It was not displayed. The original was later lost, and the versions now held by museums are replicas that Duchamp authorised decades afterwards.

The episode is usually told as a story about the definition of art, but it is equally a story about value. Nothing in the urinal's material or craftsmanship explains why its replicas are now treasured by major museums. Whatever value it has was conferred, not manufactured, and the interesting question is who did the conferring.

Philosophers have tried to name the conferrers. In the nineteen sixties, Arthur Danto argued that seeing something as art requires an artworld: an atmosphere of theory and a knowledge of art's history. George Dickie later developed an institutional theory, on which an artwork is, roughly, an artifact presented to an artworld public. Both views explain how an ordinary object can become art; neither, taken alone, explains why one such object should be worth more than another.

The market supplies a blunter answer. Prices for contemporary work are shaped by dealers, collectors, auction houses and critics whose judgements can reinforce one another, so that a reputation may become valuable partly because it is already valuable. Sceptics call this a bubble; defenders call it a conversation. The two descriptions may fit exactly the same facts, which is precisely what makes the argument so hard to settle.

None of this proves that modern art is a confidence trick. It suggests instead that artistic value has long been partly social, and that Duchamp's gesture did not create this condition so much as make it impossible to ignore. Those who dismiss a work because 'anyone could have made it' are, in a sense, agreeing with him: the making was never the whole point.
